title: How to Organize a Small Kitchen With ADHD (Tiny Space, Big Relief)
description: Small kitchen, lots of stuff, ADHD brain? Here's a 5-step system for tiny kitchens plus 7 space-saving Amazon finds that actually fit.
intro:
A tiny kitchen and an ADHD brain is a spicy combination. There's nowhere to put anything, so everything goes everywhere, and every counter becomes a staging area for things that never get staged.

But small kitchens have one secret advantage: there's less to maintain. Once each thing has a home, a small kitchen resets faster than a big one.

Here's the step-by-step plan for making a small kitchen work *with* your brain instead of against it.

sections.heading: Step 1: Edit before you organize
sections.body:
In a small kitchen, every square inch is prime real estate. So before you buy anything, pull out the extras:

- Duplicate spatulas, can openers and measuring cups (keep your favorite one)
- Mugs beyond what you use in a week
- Gadgets you've used once. Hi, spiralizer.
- Takeout containers without lids

Set a 15-minute timer and do one drawer and one cabinet. You'll be shocked how much space appears.

sections.heading: Step 2: Clear counters, except for daily stuff
sections.body:
The counters in a tiny kitchen are your workspace. Keep only what you use every single day out on them: maybe the coffee maker, a knife block and a sponge caddy.

Everything else gets a home off the counter. Clear counters mean you can actually cook, and wiping them takes ten seconds instead of moving twelve things first.

sections.heading: Step 3: Go vertical everywhere
sections.body:
When you can't go wider, go up:

- **Cabinet shelf risers** turn one tall shelf into two.
- **Under-shelf baskets** use the dead air between shelves.
- **Magnetic strips** hold knives or spice tins on the wall.
- **Over-the-door organizers** on the pantry or cabinet door hold wraps, spices or snacks.

Most small kitchens have tons of unused vertical space. It's the easiest storage you'll ever add.

sections.heading: Step 4: Use the weird spaces
sections.body:
Check these spots:

- The gap next to the fridge (slim rolling cart)
- Under the sink (two-tier pull-out organizer)
- The side of the fridge (magnetic hooks or a paper towel holder)
- Above the cabinets (baskets for rarely used stuff)

Each one might hold only a few things, but in a small kitchen, a few things is a lot.

sections.heading: Label like nobody's watching
sections.body:
In a small kitchen, things get shuffled constantly because space is tight. Labels keep everyone (including future you) putting things back in the same spot. Masking tape and a marker work fine. So does a label maker if you want the dopamine hit.

Label the shelf edge, not only the bin, so the spot stays claimed even when the bin is out on the counter.

sections.heading: Step 5: The 5-minute nightly reset
sections.body:
A small kitchen gets overwhelmed fast, but it also recovers fast. Every night, set a five-minute timer:

1. Dishes into the dishwasher or sink.
2. Anything on the counter goes back to its zone.
3. Wipe counters.
4. Start the dishwasher if it's full.

Five minutes. You'll wake up to a kitchen that feels like a fresh start instead of yesterday's problem.

outro:
Small kitchens don't need big makeovers. Edit one drawer, add one riser, and do the five-minute reset tonight.
